la:noun:campus.gloss: Open flat level ground: a plain, a natural field
senses: Open flat level ground: a plain, a natural field
a specific plain or field north of Rome’s walls called the Campus Mārtius, where the comitia centuriata were held
A field of debate: a topic
The campus of a university, college, or business
la:noun:campus.html:
campus, i, m.
cf. κῆπος, Dor. κᾶπος; perh. for scampus from σκάπτω, to dig, scabo; whence Campania, and perh. Capua; for the inserted m, cf. AAB-' λαμβάνω
.
In gen.
Lit., of any open, level land, without reference to cultivation or use, an even, flat place, a plain, field (freq. and class.; cf.: ager, planities, aequor; opp. mons, collis, silva, etc.; cf. Doed. Syn. III. p. 8 sq.): saxum plani raptim petit aequora campi,; cf. : in camporum patentium aequoribus,: aequor campi,; : aequo dare se campo,: in aequo campi,: campos pedibus transire,; cf. : campos et montes peragrantes,; cf. : spatia frugifera atque immensa camporum,; ; : campus in prata et arva salictaque et arundineta digestus,; cf. ; ; ; : virentes,: frequens herbis et fertilis ubere,: gramineus,; : pingues Asiae,: redeunt jam gramina campis, : herbosus,: herbidus aquosusque,: opimus, id'. 31, 41, 7: campi frumenti ac pecoris et omnium copiā rerum opulenti,: pigri,— Campus, like ager, is used in a wider or more restricted sense, as conveying a particular or more general idea: in agro publico campi duo milia jugerum immunia possidere,: agros Vaticanum et Pupinium, cum suis opimis atque uberibus campis conferendos,: si pinguis agros metabere campi, and 276; : certamina magna per campos instructa,: campus terrenus,: dimicaturum puro ac patenti campo,: (praefecti regii) suas copias in campum Marathona deduxerunt,: numquam in campo (in the free, open field) sui fecit potestatem, ; so ; ; cf. : insistere Bedriacensibus campis ac vestigia recentis victoriae lustrare oculis concupivit (Vitellius),; so, Bebriaci Campo spolium affectare,the battlefield,: campum colligere,.—
Meton., the produce of the field: moriturque ad sibila (serpentis) campus,.—
Poet. like aequor, in gen., any level surface (of the sea, a rock, etc.): caeruleos per campos,: campi natantes,; ; : liquentes,; : campus Liberioris aquae,; : latus aquarum,; 11, 356: immotā attollitur undā Campus (i. e. saxum),.—
Trop.: feratur eloquentia non semitis sed campis,on the open field,: (oratio) aequo congressa campo,on a fair field,: velut campum nacti expositionis,.—
Esp.
As geog. designation.
Campi Alēii, a plain in Lycia, .—
Campi Lăpĭdĕi, a stony plain near Marseilles, now La Crau, ; ; .—
Campi Ma-cri, a district in Gallia Cisalpina, on the river Macra, , prooem. § 6; ; .—
Campi Magni, in Africa, Enn. ap. (cf. Vahl. p. 167); .—
Campi Vĕtĕres, in Lucania, .—
An open place in or near Rome.
Campus Esquĭlīnus, on the Esquiline Hill, ; .—
Campus Flāmĭnĭus, on which stood the Circus Flaminius, Müll. —
Campus Scĕlĕrātus, near the Colline Gate, ; Müll. —
Far more freq. Campus, a grassy plain in Rome along the Tiber, in the ninth district, orig. belonging to the Tarquinii, after whose expulsion it was consecrated to Mars (); hence fully called Campus Martĭus, a place of assembly for the Roman people at the comitia centuriata, ; ; ; ; —Hence,
Meton., the comitia themselves: curiam pro senatu, campum pro comitiis,: fors domina campi,: venalis,; also, much resorted to by the Romans for games, exercise, and recreation, a place for military drills, etc. (cf. campicursio and campidoctor), ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—
Trop., a place of action, a field, a theatre, opportunity, subject for debate, etc. (cf. area) (a favorite figure of Cic.): me ex hoc ut ita dicam campo aequitatis ad istas verborum angustias revocas,: cum sit campus, in quo exsultare possit oratio, cur eam tantas in angustias et in Stoicorum dumeta compellimus?; cf. : in hoc tanto tamque immenso campo cum liceat oratori vagari libere,: magnus est in re publicā campus, multis apertus cursus ad laudem,: nullum vobis sors campum dedit, in quo excurrere virtus cognoscique posset,; : honoris et gloriae campus, id.

: rhetorum campus de Marathone, Salamine, Plataeis, etc.,; .

la:noun:caminus.html:
cămīnus, i, m., = ἡ κάμινος [Germ. Kamin; Fr. chemine/e; Engl. chimney],
a furnace.
A smelting-furnace for the working of metals, a forge, ; ; ; : crescunt (patrimonia) incude assiduā semperque ardente camino, i. e.,by incessant labor,.—
Poet., the forge or smithy of Vulcan and the Cyclopes, under Ætna, ; ; ; ; .—
A furnace for heating an apartment, ; .—Hence,
Meton. = ignis, fire: camino luculento uti,; ; .—
Prov.: oleum addere camino,to pour oil upon the fire, to aggravate an evil,.

la:other:Camillus.html:
cămillus (also casmilus; cf. Camena and Müll.), i, m.
with difficulty connected with the Samothracian Kabiren-Hermes, Κάδμιλος and Κάδμος; cf. Müll., and ; perh. dim. from root of Camena; cf. carmen
,
a noble youth employed in the sacrifices of the Flamen Dialis, and then, gen., in religious offices, Paul. ex Müll.: hiberno pulvere, verno luto, grandia farra Camille metes, Poët. . —The same verse is given with the expl., Camillus adulescens est, by : Romani pueros et puellas nobiles et investes Camillos et Camillas appellant, flaminicarum et flaminum praeministros,; repeated by ; cf. also Paul. ex Müll. s. v. cumeram.—
= pusillus, small, .—
